extracted.intended_audience: community college staff, faculty, and nonprofit grant writers seeking basic grant-writing guidance
extracted.subtask_description: A basic, practical guide to researching, designing, writing, budgeting, packaging, and submitting grant proposals to public and private funders, aimed at community colleges and nonprofits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government funding characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Characteristics of government funding: it is a slow process; currently there are reduced grant programs through government agencies; there are specific grant deadlines for each grant program as well as specific procedures for review of grant applications; grant program priorities and funding levels are determined each year by Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sources for identifying federal opportunities: the Federal Register (notices of availability of funding) and the Commerce Business Daily (procurement invitations, contract awards). For state opportunities use state registers; local monitoring via telephone/personal contact. Emphasize careful research to identify good prospects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundations: types and characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Private foundations are nonprofit organizations managed by a board to give financial support to qualifying organizations; classifications include family/independent, corporate/company-sponsored, community, and special purpose foundations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristics of foundation giving: is based on established priorities; accepts proposals; decides by approval of governing board; often is a one-time grant. Provide examples (e.g., Ford, Mellon) and note over 26,000 foundations exist. Use Foundation Center directories to research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate giving characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporate giving occurs via corporate foundations or corporate contributions and goes to a wide range of causes; corporate giving is evaluated in business terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristics: visibility through contributions is important; contributions follow corporate fiscal year; annual budgeted amount for new projects; not always handled by PR; proximity to corporation helps; corporate giving can include non-cash support and employee involvement. Note only ~20% of corporations give—therefore potential is large.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civic group funding characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Local civic groups (Rotary, Lions, churches, women's groups) vary in money/time/commitment but are good local fundraising sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compile/update list annually. Seek speaking opportunities or presentations to the group before requesting funds. Some groups provide volunteers or underwrite special events rather than cash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual donor characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals are the major source of philanthropic contributions (about 85% of philanthropic dollars) and give according to personal interest and preference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individual gifts range widely; gifts can be cash, goods, auction items, or volunteer time. Information on potential donors can be found in Who's Who, social registers, arts organization lists, newspapers. Individuals give to organizations needing personal attention—cultivate relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences between public and private proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: Key differences: public (government) proposals are usually very long, require forms, have strict deadlines, bureaucratic/formal style, and typically require program-specific budgets; private proposals often start with a 1–2 page letter, have fewer forms, fewer deadlines, more journalistic writing style, and may ask for additional organizational budgets/audits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match proposal length, form-completion, deadline observance, and writing style to the funder type. Federal sources use standard forms; private funders may accept inquiry letters first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and persuasive criteria of a proposal
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposal is a written representation of a program to be implemented in the future; it must provide information that clearly describes what the new program will do in chronological sequence and specify activities, individuals, organizations, and funds necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good proposal is: essential to the population served; well-planned and logical; competently staffed; producing significant, far-reaching benefits; supported by other organizations/community programs; and cost-effective. Treat the proposal as a promise and an instrument of persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of grants and proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: Types of grants include program, equipment, training, planning, and research grants. Types of proposal submissions include the proposal/inquiry letter and the full-blown grant proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the submission type appropriate to the funder (many private funders want a concise inquiry letter first; government funders usually require full proposals and forms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant-writing process checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Stepwise process: identify funding source; research and obtain guidelines; read guidelines for emphasis; develop work plan and outline; brainstorm ideas and budget; perform research; organize ideas; write draft and budget; assemble attachments and forms; review and edit with multiple reviewers; finalize forms, proofread, prepare summary/cover/TOC; package and submit by deadline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow guidelines exactly; use multiple reviewers; leave time for proofreading and packaging; type final forms only after edits are complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style and tone consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: The style and tone set in the first section must be followed throughout the proposal for consistency and clarity. Choice between first/second person (personalized) vs third person (institutional) must be maintained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer third person/institutional style for most proposals unless a small funder expects informality. Ensure section-to-section flow and consistency in voice and formality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your audience and purpose before writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Before writing, know: who will review the grant; why you are writing; what results you want; what questions the program will answer; and what activities the program will involve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spend time clarifying project goals and audience prior to drafting. Use a start-up sheet or other method to organize answers to these core questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods for developing ideas/organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods include a Start-Up Sheet questionnaire, Post-It-Note approach, traditional outline, brainstorming, and index cards for research notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the method that fits the team's working style; keep source/page references on index cards for accurate citation; use Post-Its or cards to reorder points until logical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program design planning questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Key questions for program design: What will the program do? Who will operate it (how many, types of professionals, oversight, time commitment)? When will it start/end? Who will be served and their characteristics? What are the objectives? How much will it cost? Where will it take place? What significance/importance does the project have? Why is the money needed?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hold a focused meeting of principal staff to answer these questions; record or tape sessions; use answers to create the factual basis for narrative sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordering the proposal narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested order within sections: attention-getting lead-in to issues and importance; main body supporting issues; restate major thesis as conclusion and relate to the proposed program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present supporting detail in logical, chronological or sequential order and in descending order of importance. Use an outline matching required RFP format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposal/inquiry letter structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Inquiry letter outline: I. Summary (WHO, WHERE, WHY, WHAT, WHEN, HOW MUCH); II. Background on organization; III. Needs statement (WHY); IV. Description of fundraising project (WHAT/WHEN/RESULTS/COST); V. Fundraising plan (WHEN/WHERE/FROM WHOM); VI. Request (HOW MUCH) and list of attachments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep letter brief (2–3 pages), concise, and organized. Include attachments such as board list, budget, brochure, letters of support, and architectural drawings if relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full proposal component: introduction & organizational capability
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduction and capability statement should describe the proposing organization, state mission/purpose, and build credibility rather than dwell on program details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include years in operation (or reason for creation if new), success/history, staff description, community resources, references to credibility, size of clientele, publications, major accomplishments, important events, and supportive quote(s) from letters of support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of problem/need: scope and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The needs section states the program need and provides demographic/statistical documentation; limit discussion to the problem the proposed project will address and present statistics concisely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vague, unsubstantiated generalities; use concise statistics, charts/graphs/maps/tables when possible; document limitations of existing programs and explain how the proposed project complements or improves on them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documenting need: quantitative documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative documentation presents statistical information to support need with specific factual statements rather than general statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete numbers (examples provided contrasting general vs specific statements). Use charts/graphs/maps/tables for pictorial representation and cite sources/references for statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documenting need: evidence of demand and references
rubrics_metrics.description: Document demand using market surveys, community reports or meeting results; use references wherever possible to cite sources for statistics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List compatible existing programs and their limitations; demonstrate documented demand to support the proposal's necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goals and objectives: definitions and drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: Goals are few, broad, conceptual, long-term, not easily measurable; objectives are specific, measurable, short-term outcomes from which evaluation can determine achievement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit goals (few; if more than five reconsider). Write objectives as outcomes (start with verbs like 'to increase', 'to reduce'), specify who will do what and measurable amounts, and avoid confusing methods ('to provide') with objectives. Break objectives into action steps/time-line for large projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action steps / timeline planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Where appropriate, break objectives into activities and action steps and present goals/objectives/action steps on a timeline chart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a time-line chart showing Goal / Objective / Action Step / Time Line to demonstrate feasibility and scheduling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project methodology and plan of action
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe in detail the methodology: plan of action, how objectives relate to purpose, participant selection, program operation, and partnering organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain procedures, recruitment/selection, sequence of activities, and integration with other organizations; demonstrate logical linkage between activities and objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personnel, organizational structure and staffing patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe organizational chart, board and committees, staffing pattern for the project, level of effort for each position, duties/responsibilities, and qualifications of staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include job descriptions and resumes for key staff in the appendix. Indicate percent time and months for each staff member and justify staff choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Results and benefits (project impact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe short- and long-term results and benefits such as number served, new products, problems addressed, future consequences, community/regional/national impact, and contribution to field/policy/practice/theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify expected outcomes where possible and link outcomes directly to objectives and evaluation methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Future funding / sustainability
rubrics_metrics.description: Most funders want a plan for funding after the grant ends; show how the program will be sustained or document other funders' commitments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe fees for services, ongoing fundraising campaigns, expressed interest from other funders, and provide operating budgets, audits, and investment/property information if required. Foundations often avoid funding programs without a clear sustainability plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation: program and process evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Include an evaluation section describing how you will evaluate the program (program evaluation) and/or how the program was conducted (process evaluation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program evaluation measures extent objectives were achieved and attribution to program; process evaluation measures fidelity to plan and relationship of activities to effectiveness. Prefer an external evaluator for objectivity. Consider cost, selection, evaluator participation in design, credentials, criteria, data-gathering methods, test instruments, data analysis, use of results, and reporting schedule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget: qualities and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A budget is an estimate of project costs and should be specific, detailed, informative, and contain correct addition. Include both income and expense budgets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List income sources by source and itemize expense categories: personnel (title, salary, percent time, months), fringe benefits (list items like Social Security, insurance, etc.), consultants (itemize hours/rate), space costs (sq ft x rate), equipment (itemize), supplies (itemize or monthly), travel (in-state/out-of-state with formulas), other costs (telephone, postage, printing), and indirect costs (apply negotiated percentage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: A budget narrative is a narrative description explaining the items in the budget and should always be written and placed behind the budget.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the narrative to justify salaries, travel needs, equipment purchases, and explain calculation methods so reviewers understand rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover letter/transmittal contents
rubrics_metrics.description: Cover letter should formally submit the proposal and include: name of organization, concise summary of proposed program/study, amount requested, brief statement of interest and capabilities of the organization, and contact name/address/phone/title for additional information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use organization stationery and have the CEO or Board Chair sign. Keep it brief and designate a contact person for follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title page contents
rubrics_metrics.description: Title page should provide basic identifying details: title of proposal, agency receiving the proposal, program under which submitted, proposer name/address/phone (and organizational name), and date of submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a title page even if funder does not provide one (unless prohibited). Federal/state/local funders often require specific cover/title pages—follow their format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table of contents formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a separate TOC page for proposals over ~10 pages or with many attachments; include major sections and significant attachments with page numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use formal outline numbering (Roman numerals, capital letters, Arabic numbers, lower-case letters) matching proposal headings. Ensure headings in TOC match text exactly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive summary guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: For long proposals include a concise one-page summary/abstract describing essential components; for short proposals make the first paragraph a summary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the summary last. It should answer Who? What? When? Why? Where? How Much? Keep it well-written to capture reviewer interest; length guidance: 1 page for long proposals, first paragraph for 1–5 page proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms and form-filling best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Many funders (especially federal) require forms. Make a copy to draft answers, review drafts carefully, and don't type final forms until thoroughly proofed. Submit originals if possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copy forms so you can prepare accurate responses; ensure neatness and accuracy on final submitted forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attachments and appendix contents
rubrics_metrics.description: Include supporting documents in the appendix behind the narrative: annual reports, charts/graphs, publications, pertinent studies, reference lists, board lists, contracts, operating budgets, letters of support, job descriptions, resumes, organizational chart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only include relevant attachments requested or that strengthen the application; label and reference attachments in the main text/TOC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing checklist and clarity criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Editing criteria: clarity (facts stated, easy language, appropriate to audience), style (flow), tone (friendly/personal/formal as required), clear explanations, readability, completeness, presentation (visual attractiveness, spacing), format, mechanics (spelling, grammar, punctuation), accuracy (verified statistics), consistency, and positive approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to edit while drafting; complete a full draft then edit. Use the checklist to systematically review the draft; ensure principal idea is highlighted and supporting detail is logical and ordered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Packaging and presentation guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Packaging guidance: use lots of white space; consistent margins; consider right-hand justification pros/cons; use legible type (avoid script/dot-matrix); avoid dangling lines on pages; follow funder guidance on covers/binders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose type that is easy on the eye (avoid fonts without extenders); ensure last lines of paragraphs are not left alone at top of next page; follow explicit packaging instructions from funder (staple vs bind vs covers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples and sample components usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use provided sample documents (proposal letter, title page, TOC, budget, timeline, budget narrative) as templates and examples for formatting and content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt samples to match funder guidelines and project specifics; use sample budgets and timeline charts to illustrate feasibility and calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appendix recommendations and foundation research
rubrics_metrics.description: Appendix should include lists of largest foundations (national and state), sample proposal components, sample budget, and editing checklist; use Foundation Center and other directories to research funder assets and priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a tailored appendix of local/state foundation prospects and use foundation assets/priorities to target proposals appropriately.
